sections.headline: Comfort without compromising character
sections.subline: Lewisburg's federal-style homes need HVAC solutions that respect preservation rules.

sections.heading: Why federal townhouses demand different thinking
paras: The brick facades lining Market Street represent one of the most intact early-19th-century streetscapes in central Pennsylvania. These three-story federal townhouses—narrow-fronted, with dormer windows and symmetrical details—are protected under local preservation ordinances that restrict exterior modifications. You can't mount a condenser unit on the front wall or in a side yard visible from the public right-of-way. This creates a practical problem: where does the equipment go? Rear courtyards work if you have one. Rooftops are technically possible but expensive and rarely approved. The result is that many homeowners still rely on window units, fans, or accept that central air isn't compatible with living here. The good news: ductless mini-splits and thoughtful heating upgrades can deliver modern comfort while staying compliant.

features.title: Ductless mini-splits
features.text: Rear-yard or courtyard condensers with indoor heads sized for each floor. Minimal building penetration, flexible placement, both heating and cooling.

features.title: Radiator system upgrades
features.text: Modern condensing boilers feeding existing cast-iron radiators or new baseboard. High-efficiency, silent operation, appropriate to the building's age.

features.title: Compliant window units
features.text: Rear-facing, seasonal installation with proper support and sealing. Lowest upfront cost, removable, works for single rooms or rental units.

features.title: Rooftop systems
features.text: Possible with vertical line-set routing and access provisions. Costly, requires Board approval, best suited to homes with deep setbacks.

sections.heading: Condenser placement in preservation zones
paras: Lewisburg's Historic Architectural Review Board operates under guidelines that prioritize reversibility and minimal visual impact. Any exterior modification affecting building appearance from a public street requires Board review. Condenser units fall squarely under this jurisdiction because they're large, mechanical, and visually inconsistent with 19th-century architecture. The Board's preference is rear-yard placement, screened by fencing or plantings, at least 10 feet behind the rear wall. This works in homes with deep lots and alley access. Many Market Street townhouses have shallow lots—20 to 30 feet total—and the only access is through the house. Carrying a 200-pound condenser through narrow interior doorways and steep stairs is impractical, so placement often requires a crane lift from the street. This adds $600 to $1,200 to installation cost but keeps the equipment out of sight and makes the installation compliant.

Courtyard placement is the next-best option. Many federal townhouses have walled courtyards where a condenser can be positioned out of sight from the street. The courtyard walls are typically 6 to 8 feet tall—high enough to screen a 3-foot condenser—and proximity to the house keeps refrigerant line runs short and efficient. The challenge is drainage and airflow. Condensers discharge hot air during cooling operation, and if the courtyard is enclosed on three sides with minimal ventilation, the discharged air recirculates and reduces efficiency. Positioning the unit so its discharge faces an open side of the courtyard solves this. Condensate from the indoor unit also needs to drain—either to a basement floor drain, a sump, or a drywell in the courtyard—and routing condensate lines through thick brick walls requires core drilling and careful sealing to prevent water infiltration.

sections.heading: Radiator heating and boiler upgrades
paras: Most federal townhouses in Lewisburg were originally heated by fireplaces, later converted to coal-fired boilers feeding cast-iron radiators. Many radiator systems are still in place, though the boilers have been replaced multiple times. Modern condensing gas boilers are compact, efficient, and capable of delivering 95% AFUE, but integrating them with old radiator networks requires careful balancing. The radiators were sized for steam or high-temperature hot water—180°F—and modern boilers often operate at lower temperatures to maximize efficiency. This means radiators may not deliver as much heat as originally, and rooms farthest from the boiler may run cool. The solution is upgrading the boiler's circulator pump, adding zone valves for room-by-room control, or replacing undersized radiators with larger units. Boiler replacement in a federal townhouse typically costs $6,000 to $10,000 including installation, and venting is a major consideration. Older boilers used masonry chimneys, but modern condensing boilers vent through PVC horizontally through the foundation wall. The termination has to be at least 12 inches above grade and 4 feet from windows or air intakes, which can be difficult in narrow townhouse lots where basement windows are close to the sidewalk.

Baseboard hot water heat is common in homes where original radiators were removed during renovations. Baseboard is less visually intrusive than radiators but also less effective. Baseboard delivers about 500 BTUs per linear foot at standard temperatures, so a 10-foot wall with baseboard provides 5,000 BTUs. A single cast-iron radiator can deliver 8,000 to 12,000 BTUs depending on size. Switching from radiators to baseboard often requires more linear feet of baseboard than available wall space. In small rooms or rooms with large windows, you run out of wall before meeting the heating load. The result is a room that's persistently cold in winter while the thermostat in the hallway says 70°F. Fixing this requires adding supplemental heat or reinstalling larger radiators, often sourced from salvage markets or as expensive reproduction cast iron.

sections.heading: What ductless systems cost and deliver

cards.title: System investment
cards.text: $12,000–$18,000 installed for a three-story townhouse, depending on number of indoor heads and line-set routing complexity. Both heating and cooling from one system.

cards.title: Visual trade-off
cards.text: Indoor heads are visible—plastic rectangles 10–30 inches wide, mounted 6–7 feet above the floor. Ceiling-cassette and floor-console options reduce visual impact but add cost.

cards.title: Efficiency in winter
cards.text: Mini-split heat pumps lose efficiency below 20°F. Most homeowners retain their existing gas boiler as primary heat and use mini-splits for shoulder seasons and AC.

cards.title: No ductwork needed
cards.text: Eliminates need for hidden duct runs in brick walls. Each indoor unit requires only a 3-inch wall penetration for lines and condensate drain—reversible if removed.

sections.heading: Questions about HVAC in Lewisburg's historic district

items.q: Can I install a condenser unit in my front yard if screened by shrubs?
items.a: Probably not. Lewisburg's Historic Architectural Review Board generally prohibits condenser units visible from the street, even with screening. Plantings can be removed or die, and the Board's position is that mechanical equipment shouldn't be visible regardless. Rear-yard or courtyard placement is required.

items.q: How much does it cost to add air conditioning to a federal townhouse?
items.a: Expect $12,000 to $20,000 for a ductless mini-split system serving a three-story townhouse, including outdoor condenser, indoor heads for each floor, refrigerant line routing, electrical work, and compliant installation. Costs increase if the condenser requires crane placement or if custom concealment is needed.

items.q: Are window air conditioners allowed in the historic district?
items.a: Technically no if visible from the street. Enforcement is inconsistent—many homes have window units—but the Board's position is that they're inappropriate and should be removed or relocated to rear windows. If you install one, choose a rear-facing window and remove it in winter.

items.q: What if my radiators are original and I want to keep them?
items.a: You can. Upgrading the boiler to a modern condensing model while keeping the radiators is common in Lewisburg. The radiators may need balancing or supplemental zones to heat evenly, and if they're damaged or undersized, replacement is sometimes necessary. A local contractor can assess them.

items.q: Do I need Historic Board approval for HVAC work?
items.a: Yes, if the work affects the appearance of the building from a public street. This includes condenser placement, roof penetrations, exterior venting, and visible line-set routing. Interior boiler replacement or ductless line sets routed only through the rear typically don't require approval, but it's wise to check with the Board before designing the system.

sections.heading: Balancing preservation and livability
paras: Lewisburg's preservation rules exist to protect the streetscape that makes the town architecturally significant, and most residents understand that living in the historic district means accepting certain constraints. The challenge is that the constraints fall unevenly. Homeowners with deep lots, rear access, and financial resources can install compliant ductless systems with rear-yard condensers and enjoy modern comfort. Homeowners in narrow townhouses with shallow lots, no alley access, and limited budgets end up with window units or no air conditioning at all. The preservation ordinance could be updated to allow more flexibility—for example, permitting side-yard condensers with screening or exempting rear courtyards from review entirely—but the Board has historically leaned toward preservation. For prospective buyers, HVAC should be part of the due diligence. Walk the property and assess where a condenser could go, whether the lot has rear access, and what the current heating system is. These aren't deal-breakers, but they're realities of historic-district living, and ignoring them leads to frustration after closing.
